paragraphs: Yose ben Yoezer of Tzeredah: Mishnah, Avot, chapter 1; Ein Doreshin, mishnayot 3 (2 in the linked edition) and 7, with the first passage on Chagigah 16a; Sotah 9:9. Shalshelet HaKabbalah 23a writes that some call him Yosef; so too Pesachim 16a, Chagigah 18b, and Bava Batra 133b. Maimonides writes that he is mentioned only in Chagigah, chapter 2, cited above. He is also mentioned in Eduyot 8:4, three laws. Avot de-Rabbi Natan says: just as the righteous are pious, so are their animals, as evident with Abraham our father’s camels and the donkeys of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa. He disputes with his colleague Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem, who was head of the court, while he was Nasi and a priest. Yuchasin, sequence of generations: he was the pious one of the priesthood, in the Mishnah, Ein Doreshin 18b. Here the pairs begin: the first dispute among Israel’s sages, whether to lay hands on a festival. See there, 16, and Yehudah ben Tabbai. They received from Antigonos and Shimon the Righteous, or from Antigonos and his court, in 3500. Bava Batra 133b: Yosef ben Yoezer had a son who did not behave properly. He had an atticful of dinars and consecrated it. The son went and married the daughter of King Yannai’s crown-weaver. Yuchasin writes: it is puzzling that he lived in Yannai’s time. His wife gave birth, and he bought a fish for his wife who had delivered. He cut open the fish and found a pearl. He sold it to the sacred treasury’s treasurer for the ephod stones, for thirteen atticfuls of dinars. He took the seven atticfuls the treasurer held, and consecrated six to Heaven. The sages of the generation arose and wrote: ‘Yosef ben Yoezer brought in one; his son brought in six,’ and so forth; see there. Mishnah Sotah, chapter 9 (Bavli, Sotah 47): when Yosef ben Yoezer and Yose ben Yochanan died, the clusters ceased. Rashi explains: a man who has everything in him—Torah, fear of sin, and deeds of kindness—as Rashi explains in Temurah 15b. It says there that all the clusters from Moses’ days until this pair learned Torah like Moses our teacher. They objected: but they disputed about laying hands, as above. The answer is that they disagreed at the end of their years. This requires examination: whence do we know that these were three things? Perhaps Torah and kindness, or Torah and fear of sin? It appears according to Arugat HaBosem, chapter 9, whose words are: ‘According to the ancients, three is the first to be called a number, because it contains a pair and an unpaired element, two extremes and a middle, or beginning, middle, and end. “All” may properly be said of three, not fewer. Therefore the seraphim praise with a threefold sanctification, the priestly blessing is threefold, and the threefold Torah was given to a threefold people in the third month.’ End quotation. Therefore, after they expounded eshkolot as ‘a man who has everything in him,’ Rashi explained that ‘everything’ applies to no fewer than three; thus there were three things: Torah, fear of sin, and deeds of kindness. In my large work I resolved many matters through this. Here I have gone beyond the bounds of this work, because it is very necessary. In Midrash Tehillim and Bereshit Rabbah, section 65, on ‘He smelled the scent of his garments,’ I saw that Yose ben Yoezer was killed in the Greeks’ persecution. The midrash cited above says: Yakum of Tzerorot was Rabbi Yose ben Yoezer’s sister’s son. He rode a horse on the Sabbath, while they carried before him a beam upon which Rabbi Yose ben Yoezer was to be hanged. Yakum told Rabbi Yose: ‘See the horse my master has mounted me upon’—meaning, I followed my heart’s desires and prospered, while you labored all your days in Torah and the commandments you performed—‘and see your horse upon which he has mounted you,’ meaning the beam upon which he would be hanged, and so forth. He replied: ‘If so for those who do His will, how much more for those who anger Him!’ The words entered him like a serpent’s venom. He went and carried out upon himself the four court deaths: stoning, burning, the sword, and strangulation. He brought a beam, planted it in the ground, tied a cord to it, arranged wood and surrounded it with a stone wall, made a fire before it, fixed a sword in the middle, and lit the fire beneath the wood and stones. He hung himself from the beam and was strangled by the cord he had tied; the cord snapped, the sword met him, the wall fell upon him, and he was burned. Yose ben Yoezer dozed and saw the bier of Yakum, his sister’s son, flying in the air. Rabbi Yose said: ‘In a short moment this one has preceded me into the Garden of Eden.’ End quotation. גא״י [provisionally Gelilot Eretz Yisrael] writes that Yose ben Yoezer is buried in Kefar Chammam, which some say is Tzeredah.
